beats.say: Someone puts 500 rupees in a bank at 12 per cent simple interest, and leaves it for 5 years. How much is there at the end? That is called the amount.

board.text: Rs.500 at 12% simple interest for 5 years

beats.say: 12 per cent means 12 out of every 100. So every 100 rupees earns 12 rupees in one year.

board.text: Every Rs.100 earns Rs.12 in 1 year

beats.say: So how many hundreds are in 500? 500 divided by 100 is 5. That is 5 hundreds.

spec.note: Each 100 earns Rs.12 in a year

beats.say: Each of the 5 hundreds earns 12 rupees in a year. So which sum gives the interest for one year?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 5 hundreds earns 12 rupees. So that is 12 rupees, 5 times over: 5 times 12.

beats.say: 5 times 12 is 60. That is what one year earns: 60 rupees of interest.
Simple interest is steady. It earns the same 60 rupees every single year. Look at the table, one year at a time.
So we need 60, 5 times over. 5 times 60 is 300. That is the interest for all 5 years.
Grown-ups write this as a formula. The starting money is the principal. Simple interest is principal, times rate, times time in years, divided by 100.
Put our numbers in. 500 times 12 times 5, divided by 100, comes to 300. The same answer, so we can trust it.
Now, careful. The question asks for the amount after 5 years. Is 300 the amount?

choices: No: take it away from Rs.500
ask.ifNot: 300 rupees is only the interest, the extra money. The amount is everything in the bank: the 500 rupees put in at the start, plus the interest.

beats.say: 500 plus 300 is 800. So the amount after 5 years is 800 rupees.
So: find what one year earns, multiply by the number of years, and for the amount, add the interest back on to the money at the start. Now you try one!

beats.say: 15 times 6 is 90. That is what one year earns: 90 rupees of interest.
The lovely thing about simple interest: every year earns exactly the same, 90 rupees. Here it is, a year at a time.
The money stays for 2 years, so the 90 comes twice. 90 twice is 180. That is the interest for both years.
Grown-ups write this as a formula. The starting money is the principal. Simple interest is principal, times rate, times time in years, divided by 100.
Put our numbers in. 1500 times 6 times 2, divided by 100, comes to 180. The same answer, so we can trust it.
Now, careful. The question asks for the amount after 2 years. Is 180 the amount?

choices: No: take it away from Rs.1500

The test is out of 800 marks, and the student scored 15 per cent. We want the actual marks.
Per cent means out of every 100. So scoring 15 per cent means getting 15 marks for every 100 marks in the test.
Careful: that does not mean 15 marks altogether. It is 15 for every 100, and this test has 800 marks.
Let us start from an easy one. What is 10 per cent of 800?

ask.ifNot: 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10, not by 100. 800 divided by 10 is 80.

beats.say: 800 divided by 10 is 80. So 10 per cent is 80. On the bar, that is 1 piece out of 10.

spec.note: 10 equal pieces: each is 10%. Half a piece is 5%

beats.say: 5 per cent is half of 10 per cent. Half of 80 is 40.
15 per cent is 10 per cent and 5 per cent together. 80 plus 40 makes 120.
So the student scored 120 marks.
Check it another way. 800 is 8 hundreds, and each hundred gives 15. 8 times 15 is 120. Same answer.
So remember: per cent means out of every 100. Find 10 per cent by dividing by 10, then build the per cent you need from it. Now you try one!
We want 50 per cent of 1000.
Per cent means out of every 100. So 50 per cent means 50 for every 100.
Careful: the answer is not just 50. It is 50 for every 100, and we have 1000.
50 out of every 100. Which fraction is that?

ask.ifNot: 50 is half of 100. So 50 per cent is the same as one half.

beats.say: One half. So we simply halve the number. Half of 1000 is 500.

spec.note: 2 equal pieces: each is 50%

beats.say: And that is it: the answer is 500.
Let us check with hundreds. There are 10 hundreds in 1000, and each one gives 50. 10 times 50 is 500. It matches.
So remember: 50 per cent is one half. Just halve the number. Now you try one!
There are 300 students, and 75 per cent of them are girls. We want the number of girls.
Per cent means out of every 100. So 75 per cent girls means 75 girls in every 100 students.
Careful: that does not mean 75 girls altogether. It is 75 in every 100, and here there are 300 students.
75 per cent is 3 lots of 25 per cent, so let us find 25 per cent first. 25 out of every 100 is which fraction?

ask.ifNot: 4 lots of 25 make 100. So 25 per cent is 1 out of 4 equal parts, and that is one quarter.

beats.say: One quarter. And a quarter is half of a half, so we halve, and then halve again. Half of 300 is 150.
And half of 150 is 75. So 25 per cent of 300 is 75 girls.

spec.note: 4 equal pieces: each is 25%

beats.say: 75 per cent is 3 quarters, so we need 3 lots of 75. 3 times 75 is 225.
So there are 225 girls.
Check it another way. 300 is 3 hundreds, and each hundred gives 75. 3 times 75 is 225. Same answer.
So remember: 25 per cent is one quarter, and 75 per cent is 3 of those quarters. Now you try one!

Here 2000 rupees earns simple interest at 10 per cent per annum for 4 years. Per annum means each year. How much extra money does it earn?

board.text: Rs.2000 at 10% per annum for 4 years

beats.say: 10 per cent means 10 out of every 100. So every 100 rupees earns 10 rupees in one year.

board.text: Every Rs.100 earns Rs.10 in 1 year

beats.say: So how many hundreds are in 2000? 2000 divided by 100 is 20. That is 20 hundreds.

spec.note: Each 100 earns Rs.10 in a year

beats.say: Each of the 20 hundreds earns 10 rupees in a year. So which sum gives the interest for one year?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 20 hundreds earns 10 rupees. So that is 10 rupees, 20 times over: 20 times 10.

beats.say: 2 times 10 is 20. So 20 times 10 is 10 times as much: 200. That is what one year earns: 200 rupees of interest.
Simple interest is steady. It earns the same 200 rupees every single year. Look at the table, one year at a time.
So what is the interest for all 4 years?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 4 years adds another 200 rupees. So we need 200, 4 times over.

beats.say: 4 times 200 is 800. That is the interest for all 4 years.
Here is the same idea as a formula. The money at the start is called the principal. Simple interest is principal, times rate, times time, divided by 100.
Put our numbers in. 2000 times 10 times 4, divided by 100, comes to 800. The same answer, so we can trust it.
So the simple interest is 800 rupees.
Two moves. First the interest for one year, then times the number of years. Or use the formula: principal, times rate, times time, divided by 100. Your turn next!

Per cent means out of every 100. So scoring 5 per cent means getting 5 marks for every 100 marks in the test.
Careful: that does not mean 5 marks altogether. It is 5 for every 100, and this test has 500 marks.
Let us start from an easy one. What is 10 per cent of 500?

ask.ifNot: 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10, not by 100. 500 divided by 10 is 50.

beats.say: One tenth of 500 is 50, so 10 per cent is 50. Look at the bar: it is 1 of the 10 equal pieces.

spec.note: 10 equal pieces: each is 10%. Half a piece is 5%

beats.say: 5 per cent is half of 10 per cent. Half of 50 is 25.
So the student scored 25 marks.
Check it another way. 500 is 5 hundreds, and each hundred gives 5. 5 times 5 is 25. Same answer.
So remember: per cent means out of every 100. Find 10 per cent by dividing by 10, then build the per cent you need from it. Your turn next!

Two moves. First the interest for one year, then times the number of years. Or use the formula: principal, times rate, times time, divided by 100. Now you try one!
100 students in all, and 15 per cent are girls. How many girls is that?
Per cent means out of every 100. So 15 per cent girls means 15 girls in every 100 students.
Now look at the whole: it is exactly 100. So how many is 15 out of every 100 here?

ask.ifNot: When the whole is exactly 100, there is just one lot of 100. So 15 per cent of it is simply 15.

beats.say: One lot of 100 gives 15, and there is only one lot here. So 15 per cent of 100 is 15.
So there are 15 girls.
Check with the picture. Out of 100, the shaded part is 15 and the rest is 85. Together they make the whole 100.
So remember: per cent means out of every 100. When the whole is exactly 100, the per cent is the answer. Your turn next!
A test with 400 marks, and a score of 75 per cent. How many marks is that?
Per cent means out of every 100. So scoring 75 per cent means getting 75 marks for every 100 marks in the test.
Careful: that does not mean 75 marks altogether. It is 75 for every 100, and this test has 400 marks.
75 per cent is 3 lots of 25 per cent, so let us find 25 per cent first. 25 out of every 100 is which fraction?

ask.ifNot: 4 lots of 25 make 100. So 25 per cent is 1 out of 4 equal parts, and that is one quarter.

beats.say: One quarter. And a quarter is half of a half, so we halve, and then halve again. Half of 400 is 200.
And half of 200 is 100. So 25 per cent of 400 is 100 marks.

spec.note: 4 equal pieces: each is 25%

beats.say: 75 per cent is 3 quarters, so we need 3 lots of 100. 3 times 100 is 300.

board.text: Rs.2000 at 6% simple interest for 2 years

beats.say: 6 per cent means 6 out of every 100. So every 100 rupees earns 6 rupees in one year.

board.text: Every Rs.100 earns Rs.6 in 1 year

beats.say: So how many hundreds are in 2000? 2000 divided by 100 is 20. That is 20 hundreds.

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 20 hundreds earns 6 rupees. So that is 6 rupees, 20 times over: 20 times 6.

beats.say: 2 times 6 is 12. So 20 times 6 is 10 times as much: 120. That is what one year earns: 120 rupees of interest.
The lovely thing about simple interest: every year earns exactly the same, 120 rupees. Here it is, a year at a time.
The money stays for 2 years, so the 120 comes twice. 120 twice is 240. That is the interest for both years.
Grown-ups write this as a formula. The starting money is the principal. Simple interest is principal, times rate, times time in years, divided by 100.
Put our numbers in. 2000 times 6 times 2, divided by 100, comes to 240. The same answer, so we can trust it.
Now, careful. The question asks for the amount after 2 years. Is 240 the amount?

choices: No: take it away from Rs.2000
ask.ifNot: 240 rupees is only the interest, the extra money. The amount is everything in the bank: the 2000 rupees put in at the start, plus the interest.

beats.say: 2000 plus 240 is 2240. So the amount after 2 years is 2240 rupees.
So: find what one year earns, multiply by the number of years, and for the amount, add the interest back on to the money at the start. Your turn next!

Per cent means out of every 100. So scoring 5 per cent means getting 5 marks for every 100 marks in the test.
Now look at the whole: it is exactly 100. So how many is 5 out of every 100 here?

ask.ifNot: When the whole is exactly 100, there is just one lot of 100. So 5 per cent of it is simply 5.

So the student scored 5 marks.
Check with the picture. Out of 100, the shaded part is 5 and the rest is 95. Together they make the whole 100.
So remember: per cent means out of every 100. When the whole is exactly 100, the per cent is the answer. Now you try one!
In this account, 600 rupees was spent. But by mistake it was entered as income, as money coming in. The balance shows 15000 rupees, and we must put it right.

board.text: Spent Rs.600, but entered as income

beats.say: Here is the 600 in a little table: what should have happened to it, and what really happened.
Spending makes a balance go down. So the 600 should have been taken away. Instead it was added, and the balance went up.
To put it right, how many times must we take 600 away?

ask.ifNot: Taking 600 away once only removes the mistaken adding. The 600 that was really spent still has to come off after that.

beats.say: First, undo the mistake. Take away the 600 that should never have been added. 15000 minus 600 is 14400.
Careful, here is the trap: we are not finished. 14400 is the balance before any spending. The 600 that was really spent must still come off.
14400 minus 600 is 13800. So the correct balance is 13800 rupees.
Check: the mistake pushed the balance 600 the opposite way, so it is out by 2 lots of 600, which is 1200. And 15000 minus 1200 is 13800. It agrees.
So when an entry is written the opposite way round, the fix is double: once to undo it, and once to do it properly.
This time 600 rupees came in as income. But by mistake it was written as spending. The balance shows 15000 rupees, and we must put it right.

board.text: Income Rs.600, but entered as spending

beats.say: Here is the 600 in a little table: what should have happened to it, and what really happened.
Income makes a balance go up. So the 600 should have been added. Instead it was taken away, and the balance went down.
So will the correct balance be more than 15000, or less?

ask.ifNot: The 600 was money coming in, but the account treated it as money going out. So the balance shown is too small, and the correct one is bigger.

beats.say: First, undo the mistake. Put back the 600 that should never have been taken away. 15000 plus 600 is 15600.
Careful, here is the trap: we are not finished. 15600 is the balance before the income is counted. The 600 that really came in must still be added.
15600 plus 600 is 16200. So the correct balance is 16200 rupees.
Check: the mistake pushed the balance 600 the opposite way, so it is out by 2 lots of 600, which is 1200. And 15000 plus 1200 is 16200. It agrees.
So when an entry is written the opposite way round, the fix is double: once to undo it, and once to do it properly.
Neha buys 4 pens at 10 rupees each, and hands over 50 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 4 pens at Rs.10 each. Pays Rs.50.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 50 rupees pays for the pens, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the pens
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 4 pens, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 4 pens at 10 rupees each: that is 4 times 10. 4 times 10 is 40.
Careful: 40 is only the cost, not the answer. Neha paid 50. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 40 away from 50.

beats.say: Count up from 40 to 50. That is 10 more.
So Neha gets 10 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 40, plus the change, 10, should make the 50 that was paid. It does.
So a change sum takes two moves. First find the total cost. Then take it away from the money paid. Your turn next!
The bag costs Nikhil 100 rupees: that is the cost price. Then it is sold at a profit of 15 per cent. What is the selling price?
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 100 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 15 per cent. But 15 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 100 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
And here the cost price is exactly 100 rupees. So 15 out of every 100 is simply 15 rupees. That is the profit.
So the profit is 15 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 100 plus 15 is 115. So the selling price is 115 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 115 is 15 more than 100. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. You can do the next one yourself!
Riya pays 300 rupees for a laptop. That is the cost price. It is sold at a loss of 15 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 300 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
With a loss, the selling price is smaller than the cost price. So the bottom bar stops short, and the gap is the loss.
The loss is 15 per cent. But 15 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 300 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. Loss per cent is always worked out on the cost price, never on the selling price. And per cent means out of every 100.
First find 10 per cent. That is one tenth, so divide by 10. 300 divided by 10 gives 30.
5 per cent is half of 10 per cent. Half of 30 is 15.
15 per cent is 10 per cent and 5 per cent together. 30 plus 15 makes 45. That is the loss.
So the loss is 45 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 300 take away 45 is 255. So the selling price is 255 rupees.
Quick check. With a loss, the selling price must be smaller than the cost price. 255 is 45 below 300. Good.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. Now you try one!
8 sharpeners cost 24 rupees altogether. We want the cost of just one sharpener.
Picture the 24 rupees as one long bar, cut into 8 equal pieces, one piece for each sharpener. Every sharpener costs the same.
So which sum finds the cost of one sharpener?

ask.ifNot: We are sharing 24 rupees equally among 8 sharpeners. Sharing equally is dividing.

beats.say: Think of the 8 times table. 8 times what makes 24? 8 times 3 is 24.
There it is: each sharpener costs 3 rupees.
Check by building it back up. 8 sharpeners at 3 rupees each: 8 times 3 is 24. It fits.
So when you know the cost of many and want the cost of one, divide the total by how many. You can do the next one yourself!

12 pens cost 120 rupees altogether. We want the cost of just one pen.
