A profit means it is sold for more than it cost, so the bottom bar is longer. That extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 15 per cent. But 15 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 60 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
Start with the friendly one, 10 per cent. 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10. 60 divided by 10 is 6.
5 per cent is half of 10 per cent. Half of 6 is 3.
15 per cent is 10 per cent and 5 per cent together. 6 plus 3 makes 9. That is the profit.
So the profit is 9 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 60 plus 9 is 69. So the selling price is 69 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 69 is 9 more than 60. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. You can do the next one yourself!
10 stickers, and every one costs 4 rupees. How much does Aditya pay altogether?
Let us lay it out like a shop bill. One sticker costs 4 rupees, and there are 10 of them.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 10 stickers costs 4 rupees. That is 4 rupees, 10 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: Same price, 10 times, so it is a times sum. 10 times 4 is 40.
So Aditya pays 40 rupees altogether.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 40 rupees, in lots of 4 rupees, gives 10 stickers. It fits.
Remember it like this: price of one, times the number you buy, is the total cost. Your turn next!
Here is a shop sum with two parts. 6 notebooks at 7 rupees each, and Tara pays with 92 rupees. How much change?

board.text: 6 notebooks at Rs.7 each. Pays Rs.92.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 92 rupees pays for the notebooks, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the notebooks
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 6 notebooks, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 6 notebooks at 7 rupees each: that is 6 times 7. 6 times 7 is 42.
Careful: 42 is only the cost, not the answer. Tara paid 92. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 42 away from 92.

beats.say: From 92, take off the 42. That leaves 50.
So Tara gets 50 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 42, plus the change, 50, should make the 92 that was paid. It does.
So a change sum takes two moves. First find the total cost. Then take it away from the money paid. Your turn next!
Siddharth pays 100 rupees for a watch. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 30 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 100 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
With a profit, the selling price is bigger than the cost price. So the bottom bar sticks out, and the bit that sticks out is the profit.
The profit is 30 per cent. But 30 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 100 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. Profit per cent is always worked out on the cost price, never on the selling price. And per cent means out of every 100.
And here the cost price is exactly 100 rupees. So 30 out of every 100 is simply 30 rupees. That is the profit.
So the profit is 30 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 100 plus 30 is 130. So the selling price is 130 rupees.
Quick check. With a profit, the selling price must be bigger than the cost price. 130 is 30 above 100. Good.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. You can do the next one yourself!
Here is Kavya's shopping. 4 sharpeners, at 20 rupees each. We want the total cost.
A shopkeeper would write a bill like this. The price of one sharpener, how many, and a space for the cost.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 4 sharpeners costs 20 rupees. That is 20 rupees, 4 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: We multiply, because it is the same price again and again. 20 is 2 tens. So first double the 4: that is 8.
Then 10 times 8 is 80. So 4 times 20 is 80.
So the total cost is 80 rupees.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 80 rupees, in lots of 20 rupees, gives 4 sharpeners. It fits.
Remember it like this: price of one, times the number you buy, is the total cost. Now you try one!
Sahil buys 8 rulers at 6 rupees each, and hands over 63 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 8 rulers at Rs.6 each. Pays Rs.63.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 63 rupees pays for the rulers, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the rulers
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 8 rulers, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 8 rulers at 6 rupees each: that is 8 times 6. 8 times 6 is 48.
Careful: 48 is only the cost, not the answer. Sahil paid 63. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 48 away from 63.

beats.say: 63 take away 48 leaves 15.
So Sahil gets 15 rupees back.
A quick check. Cost plus change should give back the money paid: 48 plus 15 is 63. It works.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. Your turn next!
The bag costs Diya 120 rupees: that is the cost price. Then it is sold at a profit of 50 per cent. What is the selling price?
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 120 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
With a profit, the selling price is bigger than the cost price. So the bottom bar sticks out, and the bit that sticks out is the profit.
The profit is 50 per cent. But 50 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 120 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. Profit per cent is always worked out on the cost price, never on the selling price. And per cent means out of every 100.
50 per cent is 50 out of every 100, and that is exactly one half. Half of 120 is 60. That is the profit.
So the profit is 60 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 120 plus 60 is 180. So the selling price is 180 rupees.
Does that make sense? A profit should lift the selling price above the cost price, and 180 is 60 more than 120. It fits.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. You can do the next one yourself!
Neha is at the shop, buying 7 pens. Each one costs 5 rupees. Let us find the total cost.
A shopkeeper would write a bill like this. The price of one pen, how many, and a space for the cost.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 7 pens costs 5 rupees. That is 5 rupees, 7 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: We multiply, because it is the same price again and again. 7 times 5 is 35.
So Neha pays 35 rupees altogether.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 35 rupees, in lots of 5 rupees, gives 7 pens. It fits.
So for a shop sum like this, the cost of one, times how many, gives the total. Your turn next!
Nikhil buys 5 markers at 9 rupees each, and hands over 50 rupees. We want the change that comes back.

board.text: 5 markers at Rs.9 each. Pays Rs.50.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 50 rupees pays for the markers, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the markers
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 5 markers, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 5 markers at 9 rupees each: that is 5 times 9. 5 times 9 is 45.
Careful: 45 is only the cost, not the answer. Nikhil paid 50. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 45 away from 50.

beats.say: Count up from 45 to 50. That is 5 more.
So Nikhil gets 5 rupees back.
A quick check. Cost plus change should give back the money paid: 45 plus 5 is 50. It works.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. Your turn next!
Riya pays 50 rupees for a toy. That is the cost price. It is sold at a profit of 10 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Here are two bars. The top one is the cost price, 50 rupees. The bottom one is the selling price, and we do not know it yet.
With a profit, the selling price is bigger than the cost price. So the bottom bar sticks out, and the bit that sticks out is the profit.
The profit is 10 per cent. But 10 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 50 rupees.

beats.say: This is where many children slip. Profit per cent is always taken on the cost price, not the selling price. And remember, per cent means out of every 100.
10 out of every 100 is one tenth. To find a tenth, divide by 10. 50 divided by 10 is 5. That is the profit.
So the profit is 5 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 50 plus 5 is 55. So the selling price is 55 rupees.
Quick check. With a profit, the selling price must be bigger than the cost price. 55 is 5 above 50. Good.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. Your turn next!
Here is Aditya's shopping. 4 rulers, at 7 rupees each. We want the total cost.
Let us lay it out like a shop bill. One ruler costs 7 rupees, and there are 4 of them.
So which sum gives the total cost?

ask.ifNot: Every one of the 4 rulers costs 7 rupees. That is 7 rupees, 4 times over, so we multiply.

beats.say: We multiply, because it is the same price again and again. 4 times 7 is 28.
So Aditya pays 28 rupees altogether.
Let us check by sharing it back out. 28 rupees, in lots of 7 rupees, gives 4 rulers. It fits.
So for a shop sum like this, the cost of one, times how many, gives the total. Your turn next!
Here is a shop sum with two parts. 4 rulers at 4 rupees each, and Tara pays with 21 rupees. How much change?

board.text: 4 rulers at Rs.4 each. Pays Rs.21.

beats.say: Look at the bill. Some of the 21 rupees pays for the rulers, and whatever is left comes back as change.
What must we find first?

choices: the total cost of the rulers
ask.ifNot: The shopkeeper keeps the price of all 4 rulers, not just one. So first we need the total cost.

beats.say: 4 rulers at 4 rupees each: that is 4 times 4. 4 times 4 is 16.
Careful: 16 is only the cost, not the answer. Tara paid 21. So how do we find the change?

ask.ifNot: Change is what is left of the money paid, once the cost is taken out. So we take 16 away from 21.

beats.say: Count up from 16 to 21. That is 5 more.
So Tara gets 5 rupees back.
Check it the shopkeeper's way. The cost, 16, plus the change, 5, should make the 21 that was paid. It does.
Two moves, every time: work out the total cost, then subtract it from what was paid. Your turn next!
Ananya pays 300 rupees for a bicycle. That is the cost price. It is sold at a loss of 25 per cent, and we want the selling price.
Let us draw it as two bars. On top, the cost price: 300 rupees. Underneath, the selling price, which we have to find.
A loss means it is sold for less than it cost, so the bottom bar is shorter. That missing bit is the loss.
The loss is 25 per cent. But 25 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A loss is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 300 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. Loss per cent is always worked out on the cost price, never on the selling price. And per cent means out of every 100.
25 per cent is one quarter, because 4 lots of 25 make 100. To find a quarter, halve it, then halve it again. Half of 300 is 150.
And half of 150 is 75. So 25 per cent of 300 is 75 rupees. That is the loss.
So the loss is 75 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A loss means selling for less than was paid. So the loss is taken away from the cost price.

beats.say: 300 take away 75 is 225. So the selling price is 225 rupees.
Quick check. With a loss, the selling price must be smaller than the cost price. 225 is 75 below 300. Good.
So for a loss: find the per cent of the cost price, then take it away. Your turn next!
36 is 12 per cent of some number. So we have a part, and we want the whole number.
Per cent means out of every 100. So the whole number is 100 per cent, and 36 is only 12 of those 100 parts.

spec.note: The 12% piece is 36

beats.say: What is the easiest thing to find first?

ask.ifNot: We know that 12 per cent is 36. Share that 36 into 12 equal parts, and each part is 1 per cent. That is a lovely stepping stone.

beats.say: 12 per cent is 36. So 1 per cent is 36 divided by 12, which is 3.
Careful: a common slip is to find 12 per cent of 36. But 36 is already the 12 per cent. We are climbing up to the whole, not down to a smaller part.
The whole is 100 per cent, so we need 100 lots of 3. 100 times 3 is 300.
Check it. 10 per cent of 300 is 30, and 1 per cent is 3. So 12 per cent is 30 plus 3 plus 3, which is 36. It works.
So when you know a per cent of a number and want the whole number, find 1 per cent first, then multiply by 100.
A fruit seller buys oranges in two lots: 4 dozen at 12 rupees a dozen, and 2 dozen at 16 rupees a dozen. He wants a profit of 20 per cent. What price per dozen must he sell at?

board.text: 4 dozen at Rs.12, 2 dozen at Rs.16. Profit 20%.

beats.say: Let us write his buying as a bill, and add it up line by line.
4 dozen at 12 rupees: 4 times 12 is 48. And 2 dozen at 16 rupees: 2 times 16 is 32.
Altogether he paid 48 plus 32, which is 80 rupees. That is his cost price, for 4 plus 2, which is 6 dozen.
He wants a profit of 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: Profit per cent is always worked out on the cost price, on all the money he paid. That is 80 rupees.

beats.say: 10 per cent of 80 is 8, so 20 per cent is twice that: 16. His profit must be 16 rupees.
So he must collect 80 plus 16, which is 96 rupees, for all the oranges.
Careful: the question asks for the price per dozen. What do we do with the 96?

ask.ifNot: The 96 rupees is for all the oranges, and there are 6 dozen altogether. So we share 96 among 6.

beats.say: 96 divided by 6 is 16. So he sells at 16 rupees per dozen.
Check: 6 dozen at 16 rupees brings in 96 rupees. That is 16 more than the 80 he paid, and 16 is 20 per cent of 80. It fits.
So the plan was: total cost first, then add the profit worked on the cost price, then share by the number of dozens.
A vendor buys 6 toffees for 1 rupee. He wants to gain 20 per cent. So how many toffees should he give for 1 rupee when he sells?

board.text: Buys 6 toffees for Rs.1. Wants a gain of 20%.

beats.say: A single rupee is awkward to cut up, so let us use paise. 1 rupee is 100 paise. So the 6 toffees cost him 100 paise.
He wants a gain of 20 per cent. 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: A gain is always measured on the cost price, the money he paid. Here that is 100 paise.

beats.say: 20 per cent of 100 is simply 20. So for those 6 toffees he must get 100 plus 20, which is 120 paise.
So 6 toffees must sell for 120 paise. One toffee sells for 120 divided by 6, which is 20 paise.
Each toffee sells for 20 paise. How many toffees is that for 1 rupee, which is 100 paise?

ask.ifNot: How many twenties make 100? 5 twenties. So 100 paise buys 5 toffees.

beats.say: 100 divided by 20 is 5. So he must sell 5 toffees for a rupee.
Does it make sense? He buys 6 for a rupee, and sells only 5 for a rupee. Fewer toffees for the same money: that is where his gain comes from.
So when the prices are fiddly, switch to paise, find the selling price of one, and see how many fit in a rupee.
Jim buys a cat and a dog for 600 rupees each. He sells the dog at a profit of 20 per cent, and the cat at a loss of 25 per cent. How much does he get altogether?

board.text: Dog: Rs.600, profit 20%. Cat: Rs.600, loss 25%.

beats.say: Two pets, so two little sums. We find the selling price of each one, and then add them.
Start with the dog. 10 per cent of 600 is 60, so 20 per cent is 2 times 60, which is 120. That is the profit.
The dog made a profit of 120 rupees. So what did the dog sell for?

ask.ifNot: A profit means he got more than he paid. So we add the 120 on to the 600.

beats.say: 600 plus 120 is 720. The dog sold for 720 rupees.
Now the cat. 25 per cent is one quarter. Half of 600 is 300, and half of 300 is 150. So the loss is 150 rupees.
A loss means he got less than he paid. 600 take away 150 is 450. The cat sold for 450 rupees.
Now, what does the question want?

ask.ifNot: Read the last line again. It asks how much he got altogether when he sold them. So we add the two selling prices.

beats.say: 720 plus 450 is 1170. He got 1170 rupees altogether.
Check: he paid 1200 for both. He gained 120 and lost 150, so he is 30 down. And 1200 minus 30 is 1170. It agrees.
So take one pet at a time. A profit is added to the cost price, a loss is taken away. Then answer exactly what is asked.
A shirt priced at 700 rupees is sold for 651 rupees in a sale. We want the discount as a per cent.
Two bars. The top is the price on the shirt, 700 rupees. The bottom is what it sold for, 651. The gap between them is the discount.
First the discount in rupees. 700 minus 651 is 49.
Now we need 49 rupees as a per cent. A per cent of which amount?

ask.ifNot: A discount is always measured against the price before the sale. That is the 700 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the trap. The per cent is taken on the 700, the starting price, never on the 651.
Per cent means out of every 100, and 700 is 7 hundreds. So share the 49 rupees over the 7 hundreds: 49 divided by 7 is 7.
So every 100 rupees of price gets 7 rupees off. That is a discount of 7 per cent.
Check: 1 per cent of 700 is 7, so 7 per cent is 7 times 7, which is 49. That is our discount.
So for a discount per cent: find the rupees off, then ask how many that is for every 100 of the starting price.
Some money is put away at 10 per cent simple interest per annum, for 5 years. It grows to 4500 rupees. How much was put in at the start?

board.text: 10% per annum for 5 years. Amount = Rs.4500.

beats.say: Think of the starting sum as 100 per cent. Each year, it earns 10 per cent of itself.
It earns 10 per cent every year, for 5 years. How much interest is that altogether?

ask.ifNot: Simple interest earns the same each year. 10 per cent, 5 times over, is 50 per cent.

beats.say: 5 times 10 is 50. So the interest is 50 per cent of the starting sum: exactly half of it.

spec.note: Starting sum (100%) + interest (50%) = amount

beats.say: Careful now. Is 4500 the starting sum, the interest, or both together?

ask.ifNot: Amount means everything at the end: the starting sum and the interest together.

beats.say: So 4500 is the starting sum plus half as much again. That is 150 per cent: 3 equal pieces of 50 per cent.
3 equal pieces make 4500. So one piece is 4500 divided by 3, which is 1500.
The starting sum is 2 of those pieces. 2 times 1500 is 3000. So 3000 rupees was put in.
Check: 10 per cent of 3000 is 300 a year. 5 years gives 1500. And 3000 plus 1500 is 4500. It works.
So when you are given the amount, remember it is the starting sum and the interest together. Work out what per cent that is, then go back to 100 per cent.
A retailer buys from a wholesaler at 20 per cent off the list price. He then sells at 8 per cent off the list price. We want his profit per cent.

board.text: Retailer buys at 20% off the list price,
and sells at 8% off the list price.

beats.say: No price is given, so we may choose one. Let us make the list price 100 rupees, because per cents of 100 are so easy.
He buys at 20 per cent off. 20 per cent of 100 is 20, so he pays 100 minus 20, which is 80 rupees. That is his cost price.
He sells at 8 per cent off the list price. 8 per cent of 100 is 8, so he gets 100 minus 8, which is 92 rupees. That is his selling price.
His profit is the gap between the two bars: 92 minus 80, which is 12 rupees.
Now the profit per cent. 12 rupees is a profit on which amount?

ask.ifNot: Profit per cent is always worked out on the cost price, the money he paid. He paid 80 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the trap. 12 on 100 would be 12 per cent, but he did not pay 100. He paid 80, so we compare 12 with 80.
12 out of 80. Divide both by 4: that is 3 out of 20. Now multiply both by 5: 15 out of 100. So the profit is 15 per cent.
Check: 10 per cent of 80 is 8, and 5 per cent is 4. Together, 15 per cent of 80 is 12. That is our profit.
So when no price is given, choose 100. And always take the profit per cent on the cost price.
3000 rupees earns simple interest at 12 per cent per annum, which means every year, for 5 years. We want the interest.

board.text: Rs.3000 at 12% per annum for 5 years

beats.say: 12 per cent means 12 out of every 100. So every 100 rupees earns 12 rupees in one year.

board.text: Every Rs.100 earns Rs.12 in 1 year

beats.say: How many hundreds are in 3000? 3000 divided by 100 is 30. So there are 30 hundreds.
30 hundreds, each earning 12 rupees. Which sum gives the interest for one year?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 30 hundreds earns 12 rupees. So it is 12 rupees, 30 times over: 30 times 12.

beats.say: 3 times 12 is 36, so 30 times 12 is 360. One year earns 360 rupees.
Simple interest earns the same every year. Here are the 5 years, one at a time.
So we need 5 lots of 360. 5 times 300 is 1500, and 5 times 60 is 300. Together, 1800.
The formula says the same thing. Simple interest is principal, times rate, times time, divided by 100. With our numbers, it also gives 1800.
So the simple interest is 1800 rupees.
So: find the interest for one year first, then multiply by the number of years.
Last month a clock cost 10800 rupees. This month the price has dropped to 8640 rupees. We want the discount as a per cent.

board.text: Old price Rs.10800, new price Rs.8640

beats.say: Two bars: last month's price on top, and this month's price underneath. The gap is how much the price dropped.
First the drop in rupees. 10800 minus 8640 is 2160.
The drop is 2160 rupees. To make it a per cent, which price do we compare it with?

ask.ifNot: A price cut is always measured against the price before the cut. That is the old price, 10800.

beats.say: Now use our friendly 10 per cent. 10 per cent of 10800 is 10800 divided by 10, which is 1080.
Look: 1080 and 1080 make 2160. So the drop is 2 lots of 10 per cent. That is 20 per cent.
Check: 20 per cent of 10800 is 2160, and taking 2160 off 10800 gives 8640, this month's price.
So for a per cent drop: find the drop in rupees, then see how many 10 per cents of the old price fit into it.
2000 rupees is to grow to 3500 rupees, at simple interest of 5 per cent per annum. How many years will it take?

board.text: Rs.2000 grows to Rs.3500 at 5% per annum

beats.say: 3500 is the amount: the 2000 at the start, with the interest on top. So first, how much interest is needed?
3500 minus 2000 is 1500. The money must earn 1500 rupees of interest.
Now, one year. 5 per cent means every 100 rupees earns 5 rupees in a year. 2000 is 20 hundreds, so one year earns 20 times 5, which is 100 rupees.

board.text: Every Rs.100 earns Rs.5 in 1 year

beats.say: Every year adds 100 rupees of interest. Which sum gives the number of years?

ask.ifNot: Each year brings in 100 rupees, and we need 1500 rupees of interest. So we count how many hundreds fit into 1500.

beats.say: Careful: we divide the interest, 1500, not the amount, 3500. 1500 divided by 100 is 15. So it takes 15 years.
Check: 15 years at 100 rupees a year is 1500. And 2000 plus 1500 is 3500, the amount. It works.
So for the time: find the interest needed, find the interest for one year, and divide.
In 1976 there were about 250000 lions in Africa. Since then the number has gone down by 90 per cent. How many lions are there now?
All the lions of 1976 are 100 per cent. Draw them as a bar of 10 equal pieces, 10 per cent each.

spec.note: 9 pieces are gone: that is 90%

beats.say: 90 per cent of the lions are gone. What per cent are still there?

ask.ifNot: The whole is 100 per cent. Take away the 90 per cent that are gone, and 10 per cent are left.

beats.say: 100 minus 90 is 10. Careful: the question asks for the lions that are left, the 10 per cent, not the lions that are gone.
10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10. 250000 divided by 10 is 25000.
So about 25000 lions are left.
Check: the lions that are gone are 250000 minus 25000, which is 225000. That is 9 pieces of 25000, the 90 per cent. It fits.
So when something goes down by a per cent, find what per cent is left, and take that per cent of the starting number.
Sachin has played 500 games and won 49 per cent of them. From now on he wins every game. How many more wins take him to 50 per cent?

board.text: 500 games played, 49% won. Then wins every game.

beats.say: First, how many has he won so far? 1 per cent of 500 is 5. And 49 per cent is one 5 less than 50 lots of 5: 250 minus 5, which is 245.
So he has 245 wins out of 500 games. For 50 per cent, his wins must be exactly half of his games.
Half of 500 is 250, and he has 245. So are 5 more wins enough?

choices: No: the games go up too
ask.ifNot: Every extra win is also an extra game played. So the total does not stay at 500, and the halfway mark keeps moving.

beats.say: That is the trap. Try 5 more: he has 250 wins, but out of 505 games. Double 250 is only 500, not 505. So not quite half yet.
Here is a neat way to see it. Right now his losses are 500 minus 245, which is 255. He never loses again, so the losses stay at 255.
At 50 per cent, wins and losses are equal. So he needs 255 wins. He has 245, so he needs 255 minus 245: 10 more.
Check: 10 more wins gives 255 wins out of 510 games, and 255 is exactly half of 510. That is 50 per cent!
So when a total keeps growing, look for the part that stays still. Here it was the losses.
A bank pays 6 per cent per annum simple interest. 8000 rupees is deposited for 2 years. How much interest does it earn?

board.text: Rs.8000 at 6% per annum for 2 years

beats.say: Per annum means every year. And 6 per cent means 6 out of every 100. So every 100 rupees earns 6 rupees in one year.

board.text: Every Rs.100 earns Rs.6 in 1 year

beats.say: 8000 divided by 100 is 80. So the deposit is 80 hundreds.
80 hundreds, each earning 6 rupees. Which sum gives the interest for one year?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 80 hundreds earns 6 rupees. So it is 6 rupees, 80 times over: 80 times 6.

beats.say: 8 times 6 is 48, so 80 times 6 is 480. One year earns 480 rupees.
Careful not to stop at 480. That is only one year, and the money stays in the bank for 2. Simple interest earns the same again in the second year.
480 and 480 make 960. So the interest is 960 rupees.
Check with the formula: principal, times rate, times time, divided by 100. 8000 times 6 times 2, divided by 100, is 960. It matches.
So: the interest for one year first, then times the number of years.
A shopkeeper buys 6 dozen long books. He sells 3 dozen at 150 rupees a dozen, and 3 dozen at 200 rupees a dozen, and makes a profit of 180 rupees. What did he pay per dozen?

board.text: Sold 3 dozen at Rs.150 and 3 dozen at Rs.200.

beats.say: We know what he sold them for, so start there. Here is his sales bill, to add up line by line.
3 dozen at 150 rupees: 3 times 150 is 450. And 3 dozen at 200 rupees: 3 times 200 is 600.
Altogether he took in 450 plus 600, which is 1050 rupees. That is his total selling price.
His profit was 180 rupees. So what did all the books cost him?

ask.ifNot: A profit means he sold for more than he paid. So what he paid is the selling price, with the profit taken off.

beats.say: Two bars: the cost price, and the selling price, which is 180 longer. So the cost price is 1050 minus 180, which is 870 rupees.
Careful: 870 rupees is for all 6 dozen. The question asks for the rate per dozen, so we share it among 6.
870 divided by 6. 6 times 100 is 600, which leaves 270. And 6 times 45 is 270. So that is 100 and 45: 145.
So he bought the books at 145 rupees per dozen.
Check: 6 dozen at 145 rupees is 870. Add the profit of 180 and we get 1050, exactly what he sold them for.
So when you know the selling price and the profit, take the profit off to get back to the cost price.
An article is priced at 800 rupees, and it is sold at a discount of 20 per cent. We want the sale price.
A discount is money taken off the price. So the sale price is the shorter bar, and the gap between the two is the discount.
First we need the discount in rupees. It is 20 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: The discount is taken off the price on the article. So it is 20 per cent of 800.

beats.say: 10 per cent of 800 is 80. So 20 per cent is 2 times 80, which is 160. The discount is 160 rupees.
Is 160 the sale price?

ask.ifNot: 160 rupees is what comes off. The sale price is what is left of the 800 after the discount is taken away.

beats.say: 800 minus 160 is 640. So the sale price is 640 rupees.
Check it another way. With 20 per cent off, you pay the other 80 per cent. That is 8 lots of 80, which is 640. Same answer.
So for a discount: find the per cent of the price, then take it away.
4000 rupees is to double, at 12.5 per cent simple interest. How many years will that take?
The 4000 rupees must double. So how much interest has to be earned?

ask.ifNot: Double 4000 is 8000. But the money starts at 4000, so the interest only has to bring in another 4000.

beats.say: Double 4000 is 8000. Take away the 4000 we began with, and the interest needed is 4000 rupees.

spec.note: To double, the interest must equal the start

beats.say: Now one year, at 12.5 per cent. Start with 10 per cent of 4000, which is 400.
The other 2.5 per cent is a quarter of 10 per cent. A quarter of 400 is 100. So one year earns 400 plus 100, which is 500 rupees.
Each year adds 500 rupees. How many years to reach 4000? 4000 divided by 500 is 8.
Here is a lovely way to check. 8 times 12.5 is 100. So in 8 years the interest reaches 100 per cent of the money: the whole sum again.
So for doubling: the interest must equal the starting money. Find one year's interest, and divide.
There are 5 tests, each out of 80 marks. A student has 30 per cent on the first 4. He wants 35 per cent over all 5. What must he score in the 5th test?

board.text: 5 tests of 80 marks. 30% in the first 4.

beats.say: Lots of numbers, so let us put them in a table. We need the marks he has from the first 4 tests, and the marks he wants from all 5.
All 5 tests are out of 5 times 80, which is 400 marks. The first 4 tests are out of 4 times 80, which is 320.
He wants 35 per cent of 400. Per cent means out of every 100, and 400 is 4 hundreds. 4 times 35 is 140 marks.
Now the marks he already has. He scored 30 per cent, but of which total?

ask.ifNot: He scored 30 per cent in the first 4 tests only. Those 4 tests are out of 320 marks.

beats.say: 10 per cent of 320 is 32. So 30 per cent is 3 times 32, which is 96. He has 96 marks so far.
He needs 140 and he has 96. The 5th test must give the difference: 140 minus 96 is 44.
Check: 96 plus 44 is 140, and 140 out of 400 is 35 for every 100. That is 35 per cent.
So for a target per cent: find the marks needed in total, find the marks already scored, and subtract.
An article is sold for 407 rupees, and the shopkeeper makes a profit of 10 per cent. We want the cost price.
Two bars. The cost price is on top: call it 100 per cent. The selling price is longer, by the profit, which is 10 per cent of the cost price.
So the selling price, 407 rupees, is what per cent of the cost price?

ask.ifNot: The selling price is the whole cost price, 100 per cent, with the 10 per cent profit on top. That makes 110 per cent.

beats.say: Careful, here is the trap. Do not take 10 per cent of 407. The 10 per cent is of the cost price, and 407 is the selling price.
100 per cent plus 10 per cent is 110 per cent. That is 11 pieces of 10 per cent each, and together they are 407 rupees.
So one piece is 407 divided by 11. Try 37: 10 times 37 is 370, and one more 37 makes 407. So one piece is 37 rupees.
The cost price is 100 per cent, which is 10 of those pieces. 10 times 37 is 370.
Check: 10 per cent of 370 is 37, and 370 plus 37 is 407. It works.
So when you are given the selling price and the profit per cent, the selling price is 100 per cent plus the profit. Work back from there to the cost price.
Some money earns 189 rupees of simple interest in 3 years, at 9 per cent per annum. We want that sum of money.

board.text: Interest Rs.189 in 3 years at 9% per annum

beats.say: Simple interest earns the same each year. So first, the interest for just one year: 189 divided by 3 is 63.
63 rupees is one year's interest, at 9 per cent. So 63 is 9 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: The rate is always a per cent of the money at the start. So 9 per cent of the sum is 63 rupees.

beats.say: 9 per cent of the sum is 63. So 1 per cent is 63 divided by 9, which is 7 rupees.
The whole sum is 100 per cent. 100 times 7 is 700. So the sum is 700 rupees.
Careful: the slip here is to forget the years, and treat 189 as one year's interest. Always bring it down to one year first.
Check: every 100 rupees earns 9, and 700 is 7 hundreds, so one year earns 63. 3 years earn 3 times 63, which is 189. It works.
So for the sum: interest for one year first, then 1 per cent, then 100 per cent.
40 per cent of the students passed, and 420 students did not. We want the number of students who took the exam.
All the students together are 100 per cent. Let us draw them as one bar, cut into 10 equal pieces of 10 per cent each.

spec.note: 4 pieces passed, 6 pieces did not

beats.say: 420 is the number who did not pass. What per cent of the students is that?

ask.ifNot: 40 per cent passed. The rest did not, and the rest is 100 minus 40, which is 60 per cent.

beats.say: Careful, here is the trap. 420 is not the 40 per cent. It is the other part: 100 minus 40, which is 60 per cent.
60 per cent is 6 of our 10 pieces. So one piece is 420 divided by 6, which is 70.
All the students are 10 pieces. 10 times 70 is 700.
Check: one piece is 70, so the 4 pieces who passed are 280. And 700 minus 280 is 420, the ones who did not pass. It works.
So first ask: which per cent does my number really stand for? Then find one piece, and build up to the whole 100 per cent.
A student scored 72 per cent on a test of 25 questions. We want the number of answers that were not correct.
72 per cent means 72 right out of every 100. But this test has only 25 questions, and 25 is one quarter of 100.
100 questions would give 72 right. This test is a quarter of that size. So how many did he get right?

ask.ifNot: A quarter of the questions means a quarter of the right answers. And to find a quarter, we divide by 4.

beats.say: To divide by 4, halve and halve again. Half of 72 is 36, and half of 36 is 18. So he got 18 answers right.
Careful now. Is 18 our answer?

choices: No: we want the ones not correct
ask.ifNot: 18 is the number he got right. The question asks for the answers that were not correct: the rest of the 25.

beats.say: 25 questions, 18 right. 25 minus 18 is 7. So 7 answers were not correct.
Check it another way. 100 minus 72 is 28, so 28 per cent were not correct. A quarter of 28 is 7. Same answer.
So read to the very end. Find the per cent, then check whether the question wants that part, or the rest.
3200 rupees grows to 3680 rupees in 3 years, at simple interest. We want the rate of interest.

board.text: Rs.3200 amounts to Rs.3680 in 3 years

beats.say: 3680 rupees is called the amount. It is the 3200 rupees that was put in, with the interest on top.
So how do we find the interest?

ask.ifNot: The amount is the starting money and the interest together. Take the starting money away, and the interest is what is left.

beats.say: 3680 minus 3200 is 480. So the interest is 480 rupees, for all 3 years.
Careful: the rate is for one year, not for all 3. Simple interest is the same every year, so one year's interest is 480 divided by 3, which is 160.
The rate tells us what every 100 rupees earns in one year. 3200 divided by 100 is 32, so the money is 32 hundreds.

board.text: Rate = interest on each Rs.100 in 1 year

beats.say: 32 hundreds earn 160 rupees a year. 32 times 5 is 160, so each hundred earns 5 rupees.
Each 100 rupees earns 5 rupees a year. That is a rate of 5 per cent per annum.
Check with the formula: principal, times rate, times time, divided by 100. 3200 times 5 times 3, divided by 100, is 480. That is our interest.
So for the rate: amount minus principal gives the interest. Share it over the years, and then over the hundreds.
A shopkeeper buys a pen for 40 rupees: that is the cost price. He wants a profit of 25 per cent. What should the selling price be?
Two bars. The top one is the cost price, 40 rupees. The selling price is longer, and the extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 25 per cent. But 25 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: Profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 40 rupees.

beats.say: Careful: profit per cent is always worked on the cost price. And 25 per cent is one quarter, because 4 lots of 25 make 100.
A quarter of 40: half of 40 is 20, and half of 20 is 10. So the profit is 10 rupees.
The profit is 10 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 40 plus 10 is 50. So he should sell the pen for 50 rupees.
Check: the selling price, 50, is 10 more than the cost price, 40. And 4 lots of 10 make 40, so 10 really is a quarter of it.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on.
20 per cent of an electricity bill is taken off, and 100 rupees is still to be paid. We want the bill before anything was taken off.

board.text: 20% is taken off the bill. Rs.100 is left to pay.

beats.say: The whole bill is 100 per cent. Cut it into 5 equal pieces, and each piece is 20 per cent.

spec.note: 1 piece is taken off, 4 pieces are left

beats.say: One piece, 20 per cent, is taken off. So the 100 rupees left to pay is what per cent of the bill?

ask.ifNot: 100 per cent, take away 20 per cent, leaves 80 per cent. The 100 rupees is that 80 per cent.

beats.say: Careful: the 100 rupees is not the whole bill, and it is not the 20 per cent either. It is the 80 per cent that is left: 4 of the 5 pieces.
4 pieces are 100 rupees. So one piece is 100 divided by 4, which is 25 rupees.
The whole bill is 5 pieces. 5 times 25 is 125. So the bill was 125 rupees.
Check: 20 per cent of 125 is one piece, 25 rupees. And 125 minus 25 is 100, just as the question says.
So when a part is taken off, work out what per cent is left, find one piece, and build the whole.
Harry buys a saddle for 100 rupees, sells it for 200, buys it back for 300, and sells it again for 400. Did he make a profit or a loss overall?

board.text: Bought Rs.100, sold Rs.200, bought Rs.300, sold Rs.400

beats.say: Four deals, and it is easy to get muddled. So we make two columns: money Harry paid out, and money he got in.
To see how he did overall, what should we compare?

choices: all he paid with all he got
ask.ifNot: Every rupee counts. Add up everything he paid out, add up everything he got in, and then compare the two totals.

beats.say: Money paid out: 100 in April and 300 in June. 100 plus 300 is 400 rupees.
Money got in: 200 in May and 400 in July. 200 plus 400 is 600 rupees.
He got in more than he paid out, so it is a profit. 600 minus 400 is 200 rupees.
Careful with the trap here. Buying it back for 300, after selling it for 200, feels like losing 100. But the two columns tell the whole story.
Check it deal by deal. Bought at 100, sold at 200: a profit of 100. Bought at 300, sold at 400: another 100. And 100 plus 100 is 200.
So with many deals, total the money paid out, total the money got in, and compare the two.
25 rupees is to become 37 rupees, at 16 per cent per annum simple interest. How long will it take?

board.text: Rs.25 becomes Rs.37 at 16% per annum

beats.say: 37 rupees is the amount: the 25 at the start, with the interest on top. The interest needed is 37 minus 25, which is 12 rupees.
Now the interest for one year. It is 16 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: Interest is always worked on the money at the start, the principal. That is 25 rupees.

beats.say: 16 per cent means 16 rupees on every 100. But 25 is only a quarter of 100. So it earns a quarter of 16, which is 4 rupees a year.
Each year adds 4 rupees, and we need 12. 12 divided by 4 is 3. So it takes 3 years.
Check it a year at a time, in the table. 25 grows to 29, then 33, then 37. After 3 years it reaches 37 rupees.
So for the time: find the interest needed, find the interest for one year, and divide.
Kedar borrowed 12000 rupees from his friend at simple interest. After 5 years he paid back 15600 rupees to settle the loan. What rate did his friend charge?

board.text: Borrowed Rs.12000. Paid back Rs.15600 after 5 years.

beats.say: 15600 rupees is called the amount. It is the 12000 rupees that was borrowed, with the interest on top.
So how do we find the interest?

ask.ifNot: The amount is the starting money and the interest together. Take the starting money away, and the interest is what is left.

beats.say: 15600 minus 12000 is 3600. So the interest is 3600 rupees, for all 5 years.
Careful: the rate is for one year, not for all 5. Simple interest is the same every year, so one year's interest is 3600 divided by 5, which is 720.
The rate tells us what every 100 rupees earns in one year. 12000 divided by 100 is 120, so the money is 120 hundreds.

board.text: Rate = interest on each Rs.100 in 1 year

beats.say: 120 hundreds earn 720 rupees a year. 12 times 6 is 72, so 120 times 6 is 720. Each hundred earns 6 rupees.
Each 100 rupees earns 6 rupees a year. That is a rate of 6 per cent per annum.
Check with the formula: principal, times rate, times time, divided by 100. 12000 times 6 times 5, divided by 100, is 3600. That is our interest.
So for the rate: what was paid back, minus what was borrowed, is the interest. Share it over the years, and then over the hundreds.
This one sounds like a tongue twister: 5 per cent, of 5 per cent, of 100 rupees.
The trick is to start from the far end, and take one step at a time. So first: 5 per cent of 100 rupees.
Per cent means out of every 100. So 5 per cent of 100 rupees is simply 5 rupees.

spec.note: 5 out of every 100

beats.say: Now we need 5 per cent of those 5 rupees. Will that be more than 1 rupee, or less?

ask.ifNot: 5 per cent is a small part: only 5 out of every 100. A small part of just 5 rupees must be tiny, less than 1 rupee.

beats.say: Let us use paise to see it clearly. Each rupee is 100 paise, so 5 rupees is 500 paise.
10 per cent of 500 is 50, and 5 per cent is half of that: 25. So the answer is 25 paise.
25 paise is a quarter of a rupee. In rupees, we write it as 0.25.
Careful with the trap here. The two 5 per cents do not add up to 10 per cent. Each one takes its own small slice of what is in front of it.
So for a per cent of a per cent: start from the end, and take one slice at a time.
A shopkeeper sells a bat for 600 rupees, and that gives him a profit of 20 per cent. We want the cost price of the bat.
Call the cost price 100 per cent, and cut it into 5 equal pieces of 20 per cent. The profit is 20 per cent of the cost price, so the selling price is one piece longer.
How many of these equal pieces make the selling price, 600 rupees?

ask.ifNot: The cost price is 5 pieces. The profit adds 1 more piece of the same size. So the selling price is 6 pieces.

beats.say: Careful, this is the classic trap. 20 per cent of 600 is not the profit. The profit is 20 per cent of the cost price, and 600 is the selling price.
6 pieces are 600 rupees. So one piece is 600 divided by 6, which is 100 rupees.
The cost price is 5 pieces. 5 times 100 is 500. So the bat cost 500 rupees.
Check: 20 per cent of 500 is 100, and 500 plus 100 is 600, the selling price. It works.
So when the selling price and the profit per cent are given, draw the cost price as 100 per cent, add the profit pieces, and find one piece.
A man buys 1000 candy bars at 5 bars for 2 rupees. He sells them all at 2 bars for 1 rupee. We want his profit or loss as a per cent.

board.text: Buys 1000 bars at 5 for Rs.2. Sells at 2 for Rs.1.

beats.say: First, what did he pay? The bars come in groups of 5. 1000 divided by 5 is 200 groups, and each group costs 2 rupees. 200 times 2 is 400.
Now, what did he get? He sells in groups of 2. 1000 divided by 2 is 500 groups, at 1 rupee each. That is 500 rupees.
Cost price 400, selling price 500. He got more than he paid, so it is a profit. 500 minus 400 is 100 rupees.
Now the per cent. The profit of 100 rupees is compared with which amount?

ask.ifNot: Profit per cent is always worked out on the cost price, the money he paid. That is 400 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, this is the trap: comparing the profit with the selling price, 500. Profit per cent always uses the cost price. So it is 100 out of 400.
100 out of 400 is one quarter, because 4 times 100 is 400. And a quarter is 25 out of 100, which is 25 per cent.
Check: a quarter of 400 is 100, and 400 plus 100 is 500, the selling price. It fits.
So: find the total cost price, find the total selling price, and take the profit per cent on the cost price.
Aniket borrowed 18000 rupees to open a grocery shop. He cleared the loan by paying 25560 rupees at the end of 3 years. We want the rate of interest.

board.text: Borrowed Rs.18000. Paid Rs.25560 after 3 years.

beats.say: 25560 rupees is called the amount. It is the 18000 rupees that was borrowed, with the interest on top.
So how do we find the interest?

ask.ifNot: The amount is the starting money and the interest together. Take the starting money away, and the interest is what is left.

beats.say: 25560 minus 18000 is 7560. So the interest is 7560 rupees, for all 3 years.
Careful: the rate is for one year, not for all 3. Simple interest is the same every year, so one year's interest is 7560 divided by 3, which is 2520.
The rate tells us what every 100 rupees earns in one year. 18000 divided by 100 is 180, so the money is 180 hundreds.

board.text: Rate = interest on each Rs.100 in 1 year

beats.say: 180 hundreds earn 2520 rupees a year. 10 times 180 is 1800, and 4 times 180 is 720. Together that is 2520, so each hundred earns 14 rupees.
Each 100 rupees earns 14 rupees a year. That is a rate of 14 per cent per annum.
Check with the formula: principal, times rate, times time, divided by 100. 18000 times 14 times 3, divided by 100, is 7560. That is our interest.
So for the rate: what was paid, minus what was borrowed, is the interest. Share it over the years, and then over the hundreds.
A principal, the money at the start, earns 160 rupees of simple interest in 5 years, at 8 per cent per annum. We want the principal.

board.text: Interest Rs.160 in 5 years at 8% per annum

beats.say: Each year the principal earns 8 per cent of itself. Here are the 5 years, one at a time.
8 per cent every year, for 5 years. So the 160 rupees is what per cent of the principal?

ask.ifNot: Simple interest earns the same each year. 8 per cent, 5 times over, is 5 times 8, which is 40 per cent.

beats.say: 5 times 8 is 40. So 40 per cent of the principal is 160 rupees.
40 per cent is 4 lots of 10 per cent. So 10 per cent is 160 divided by 4, which is 40 rupees.
The whole principal is 100 per cent: 10 lots of 10 per cent. 10 times 40 is 400. So the principal is 400 rupees.
Careful: 160 is the interest, not the principal. The principal is the bigger sum that earned it.
Check: 8 per cent of 400 is 32 rupees a year. 5 years earn 5 times 32, which is 160. It works.
So for the principal: find what per cent the interest is altogether, then build up to 100 per cent.
An article worth 400 rupees is sold for 324 rupees. We want the loss as a per cent.

board.text: Cost price Rs.400, sold for Rs.324

beats.say: Two bars. The cost price, 400, is the longer one. The selling price, 324, is shorter, and the missing bit is the loss.
First the loss in rupees. 400 minus 324 is 76.
76 rupees were lost. To make that a per cent, we compare it with which amount?

ask.ifNot: Loss per cent, just as with profit per cent, is always worked out on the cost price. That is 400 rupees.

beats.say: Careful: it is the cost price, never the selling price. Now, per cent means out of every 100, and 400 is 4 hundreds.
So share the loss of 76 over the 4 hundreds. Half of 76 is 38, and half of 38 is 19. Each hundred loses 19 rupees.
19 lost out of every 100. So the loss is 19 per cent.
Check: 19 per cent of 400 is 4 times 19, which is 76. And 400 minus 76 is 324, the selling price.
So for a loss per cent: find the loss in rupees, then see how much that is for every 100 of the cost price.
A student needs 40 per cent to pass. He scores 94 marks, and that is 74 marks short. We want the maximum marks.
He scored 94, and he was 74 marks short of passing. So what was the pass mark?

ask.ifNot: Being 74 short means he needed 74 more marks to reach the pass mark. So the pass mark is 94 plus 74.

beats.say: 94 plus 74 is 168. So he needed 168 marks to pass.
That pass mark is 40 per cent of the maximum. The maximum is the whole, 100 per cent. Picture it as 10 equal pieces of 10 per cent.

spec.note: 4 pieces = 168 marks

beats.say: 40 per cent is 4 pieces. So one piece is 168 divided by 4, which is 42.
The maximum is all 10 pieces. 10 times 42 is 420.
Check: 4 pieces of 42 make 168, the pass mark. He scored 94, and 168 minus 94 is 74. He is short by 74, as the question says.
So: first find the pass mark. Then use it as the per cent you know, and build up to the whole.
26500 rupees is deposited in a bank at 8 per cent per annum simple interest. We want the amount at the end of 4 years: everything that is there.

board.text: Rs.26500 at 8% per annum for 4 years

beats.say: 8 per cent means 8 out of every 100. So every 100 rupees earns 8 rupees in one year.

board.text: Every Rs.100 earns Rs.8 in 1 year

beats.say: 26500 divided by 100 is 265. So there are 265 hundreds, each earning 8 rupees a year.
265 times 8, in easy bites. 200 times 8 is 1600, 60 times 8 is 480, and 5 times 8 is 40. Together, 2120 rupees a year.
Simple interest earns the same every year. 4 years, each earning 2120. 4 times 2000 is 8000, and 4 times 120 is 480. So the interest is 8480 rupees.
Careful now. The question asks for the amount. Is 8480 the answer?

ask.ifNot: 8480 rupees is only the interest, the extra money. The amount is everything in the bank: the 26500 put in, plus the interest.

beats.say: 26500 plus 8480 is 34980. So the amount is 34980 rupees.
Check the interest with the formula: principal, times rate, times time, divided by 100. It gives 8480 too.
So: interest for one year, then for all the years. And when the question says amount, add the interest on to the money at the start.
A man buys a mobile phone for 18000 rupees: that is the cost price. He wants a profit of 18 per cent. What should the selling price be?
Two bars. The top one is the cost price, 18000 rupees. The selling price is longer, and the extra bit on the end is the profit.
The profit is 18 per cent. But 18 per cent of what?

ask.ifNot: Profit is always measured against the money paid at the start. That is the cost price, 18000 rupees.

beats.say: Careful: profit per cent is always worked on the cost price. For an awkward per cent such as 18, find 1 per cent first. 18000 divided by 100 is 180.
18 per cent is 18 lots of 180. 10 times 180 is 1800, and 8 times 180 is 1440. Together, 3240. That is the profit.
The profit is 3240 rupees. How do we get the selling price?

ask.ifNot: A profit means selling for more than was paid. So the profit is added on top of the cost price.

beats.say: 18000 plus 3240 is 21240. So the selling price is 21240 rupees.
Check with a rough guess. 20 per cent of 18000 would be 3600, so 18 per cent should be a little less. 3240 is. Good.
So for a profit: find the per cent of the cost price, then add it on. And when the per cent is awkward, go through 1 per cent.
Here is a line with two per cents, and a hidden number, A. We have to find A.
One of the per cents has no letter in it, so we can work it out straight away. That is 15 per cent of 40.
10 per cent of 40 is 4, and 5 per cent is half of that, which is 2. So 15 per cent of 40 is 4 plus 2: that makes 6.
So the line now says: 6, minus 25 per cent of A, equals 2.
6 minus something leaves 2. What is the something?

ask.ifNot: Start at 6 and come down to 2. You have taken away 4. So 25 per cent of A is 4.

beats.say: 6 minus 4 is 2. So 25 per cent of A must be 4.
25 per cent is one quarter. If a quarter of A is 4, then the whole of A is 4 quarters: 4 times 4, which is 16.

spec.note: 4 quarters make the whole of A

beats.say: Careful with that last step. A common slip is to take a quarter of 4. But 4 is already the quarter, so we multiply up, not down.
Check: a quarter of 16 is 4, and 6 minus 4 is 2. It works.
So work out the per cent you can, see what the missing per cent must be, then build up to the whole.
Here is a line with a hidden number, Z, and two per cents. We want Z.
Think of the equals sign as a balance. Before we can find Z, we turn each per cent into a plain number. Start with 16 per cent of 150.
10 per cent of 150 is 15. 5 per cent is half of that, 7.5. And 1 per cent is 1.5.
16 per cent is 10 and 5 and 1 together. 15 plus 7.5 plus 1.5 makes 24.
Now 13 per cent of 600. 1 per cent of 600 is 6, so we need 13 sixes. 10 sixes are 60, and 3 sixes are 18. Together, 78.
So our line becomes: Z plus 24 equals 78. Here it is on a balance.
Z plus 24 makes 78. How do we find Z?

ask.ifNot: Z and 24 together make 78. Take the 24 away from the 78, and what is left is Z.

beats.say: 78 minus 24 is 54. So Z is 54.
Check: 54 plus 24 is 78, and 78 is 13 per cent of 600. Both sides balance.
So with a line like this, turn each per cent into a plain number first. Then it is a simple missing number sum.
6420 rupees amounts to 10272 rupees in 4 years, at simple interest. We want the rate of interest per annum.

board.text: Rs.6420 amounts to Rs.10272 in 4 years

beats.say: 10272 rupees is the amount: the 6420 rupees at the start, with the interest on top.
So how do we find the interest?

ask.ifNot: The amount is the starting money and the interest together. Take the starting money away, and the interest is what is left.

beats.say: 10272 minus 6420 is 3852. So the interest is 3852 rupees, for all 4 years.
Careful: the rate is for one year, not for all 4. Simple interest is the same each year, so one year's interest is 3852 divided by 4, which is 963.
The rate is that 963 as a per cent of the starting money. 1 per cent of 6420 is 64.2. So how many lots of 64.2 make 963?
10 lots of 64.2 make 642. 5 lots are half of that, 321. And 642 plus 321 is 963. So it is 15 lots: the rate is 15 per cent.
Before we trust it, check with the formula: principal, times rate, times time, divided by 100. It gives 3852, our interest.
So the rate is 15 per cent per annum. Now look at the choices. Which one matches?

ask.ifNot: Our rate is 15 per cent, and that is not on the list. When careful, checked working matches none of the choices, the answer is none of these.

beats.say: So the answer is none of these. The rate is 15 per cent per annum, and that is not one of the choices.
So for the rate: find the interest, bring it down to one year, then see what per cent of the starting money it is.
A principal, the money at the start, earns 2205 rupees of simple interest in 12 months, at 18 per cent per annum. We want the principal.

board.text: Interest Rs.2205 in 12 months at 18% per annum

beats.say: The rate is per annum, which means per year. How long is 12 months?

ask.ifNot: A year has 12 months. So 12 months is exactly 1 year, and 2205 rupees is one year's interest.

beats.say: 12 months is exactly 1 year. So 2205 rupees is one year's interest, and that is 18 per cent of the principal.

spec.note: The 18% piece is Rs.2205

beats.say: Here is a neat stepping stone. 18 per cent is 9 lots of 2 per cent. So 2 per cent is 2205 divided by 9.
9 times 200 is 1800. That leaves 2205 minus 1800, which is 405. And 9 times 45 is 405. So 2205 divided by 9 is 200 and 45: that is 245.
The whole principal is 100 per cent, which is 50 lots of 2 per cent. 100 times 245 is 24500, and 50 times is half of that: 12250.
So the principal is 12250 rupees.
Check: 18 per cent of 12250 should give back 2205, one year's interest. It does.
So: make sure the time is in years, then use the interest as a known per cent of the principal, and build up to 100 per cent.
An article sold for 336 rupees makes a loss of 84 rupees. We want the profit if the same article is sold for 542 rupees.

board.text: Sold for Rs.336: a loss of Rs.84.

beats.say: Both sales are of the same article. So the bridge between them is its cost price. We find that first.
It sold for 336 rupees, at a loss of 84. So was the cost price more than 336, or less?

ask.ifNot: A loss means it was sold for less than it cost. So the cost price is bigger than 336, by the 84 that was lost.

beats.say: 336 plus 84 is 420. So the cost price is 420 rupees.
Now sell the same article for 542 rupees. That is more than 420, so this time there is a profit. 542 minus 420 is 122.
Before we trust it, we check. 420 minus 84 is 336, the first sale. And 420 plus 122 is 542, the second sale. Both fit the question.
So the profit is 122 rupees. Now look at the choices. Which one matches?

ask.ifNot: Our profit is 122 rupees, and that number is not on the list. When careful, checked working matches none of the choices, the answer is none of these.

beats.say: So the answer is none of these. The profit is 122 rupees, and that is not one of the choices.
So the cost price is the bridge between two sales. And trust careful working, even when your answer is not on the list.
450 rupees is to become four times itself, at 24 per cent per annum simple interest. How long will it take?

board.text: Rs.450 becomes four times itself at 24% per annum

beats.say: The money becomes 4 times itself. How many lots of 450 must come from the interest?

ask.ifNot: There are 4 lots at the end, but 1 of them is the money we began with. So the interest must bring in the other 3 lots.

beats.say: That is the trap: one of the 4 lots is already there. So the interest needed is 3 times 450, which is 1350 rupees.

spec.note: 1 lot is the start, 3 lots are interest

beats.say: Now one year, at 24 per cent. 1 per cent of 450 is 4.5, so we need 24 lots of 4.5.
24 times 4 is 96, and 24 halves are 12. Together, 108. So one year earns 108 rupees.
How many years to earn 1350, at 108 a year? 10 years earn 1080. That leaves 1350 minus 1080, which is 270.
2 more years earn 216, which leaves 54. And 54 is exactly half of 108, so that is half a year more. 10 and 2 make 12 years, and a half.
Half a year is 6 months. So the time is 12 years 6 months.
Check: 12.5 years at 108 rupees a year comes to 1350, the interest we needed.
So when money becomes so many times itself, take away the lot you began with. The rest is interest: divide it by one year's interest.
An article is sold at a loss of 12 per cent, and that loss is 60 rupees. We want the profit per cent if it is sold at 620 rupees instead.
A loss per cent is always a per cent of the cost price. So this tells us that 12 per cent of the cost price is 60 rupees.
What is the handiest stepping stone to the whole cost price?

ask.ifNot: We know that 12 per cent is 60 rupees. Share the 60 into 12 equal parts, and each part is 1 per cent of the cost price.

beats.say: 60 divided by 12 is 5. So 1 per cent of the cost price is 5 rupees.
The whole cost price is 100 per cent. 100 times 5 is 500 rupees.
Now it is sold at 620 rupees. That is above 500, so there is a profit: 620 minus 500 is 120 rupees.
For the profit per cent, we compare the 120 rupees with which amount?

ask.ifNot: Profit per cent is always worked out on the cost price. Here that is 500 rupees.

beats.say: 1 per cent of the cost price is 5 rupees. How many 5s make 120? 120 divided by 5 is 24. So the profit is 24 per cent.
Check: 24 lots of 5 rupees: 20 times 5 is 100, and 4 times 5 is 20, which makes 120. The working holds.
Now look at the choices. 24 per cent is not among them. So the answer is none of these.
So: use the loss to find the cost price, then take the new profit per cent on that cost price. And trust careful working, even when it is not on the list.
What per cent is 84 minutes, of 7 hours?
Before we compare them, what must we fix?

ask.ifNot: 84 is in minutes and 7 is in hours. We can only compare two amounts when they are in the same unit.

beats.say: Careful: 84 divided by 7 would mix minutes with hours. Change the hours into minutes first. Each hour is 60 minutes, so 7 hours is 7 times 60: 420 minutes.
So the real question is: 84 minutes is what per cent of 420 minutes? Here are the 420 minutes, cut into 10 equal pieces of 10 per cent.

spec.note: 10 equal pieces: each is 10%

beats.say: One piece is 10 per cent of 420. Divide by 10: that is 42 minutes.
One piece is 42 minutes. How many pieces make 84 minutes?

ask.ifNot: 42 and 42 make 84. So 84 minutes is 2 of the 10 per cent pieces.

beats.say: 42 plus 42 is 84. So 84 minutes is 2 pieces of 10 per cent, and that is 20 per cent.

spec.note: 2 pieces of 42 minutes = 84 minutes

beats.say: Check: 20 per cent is one fifth, and 420 divided by 5 is 84. It fits.
So for what per cent is this of that: put them in the same units first, then see how many 10 per cents fit.
An article sold at 440 rupees gives a profit of 10 per cent. We want the selling price that would give a profit of 17 per cent.
Both selling prices belong to the same article. So the bridge between them is the cost price. Call the cost price 100 per cent.
With a 10 per cent profit, the selling price, 440, is what per cent of the cost price?

ask.ifNot: The selling price is the whole cost price, 100 per cent, with the 10 per cent profit on top. That makes 110 per cent.

beats.say: 100 per cent plus 10 per cent is 110 per cent. So 110 per cent of the cost price is 440 rupees.
Find 1 per cent: 440 divided by 110. 110 times 4 is 440, so 1 per cent of the cost price is 4 rupees.
Careful: the trap is to add 7 per cent of 440. But every profit per cent is taken on the cost price, not on the old selling price.
For a profit of 17 per cent, the selling price is 100 plus 17, which is 117 per cent of the cost price.
So we need 117 lots of 4. 100 times 4 is 400, and 17 times 4 is 68. Together, 468.
So it should be sold at 468 rupees.
Check: the cost price is 400 rupees. 17 per cent of 400 is 68, and 400 plus 68 is 468.
So to change from one profit per cent to another, go back to the cost price first, then build the new selling price.
28 per cent of a number is 196. We want 43 per cent of that same number.

spec.note: We know the 28% piece. We want a 43% piece.

beats.say: We need a stepping stone between 28 per cent and 43 per cent. What is the handiest one?

ask.ifNot: 196 is already 28 per cent of the number. Share it into 28 equal parts and each part is 1 per cent. From 1 per cent we can reach any per cent.

beats.say: So how many 28s make 196? Let us try 7. 20 times 7 is 140, and 8 times 7 is 56.
140 plus 56 is 196. It fits exactly. So 1 per cent of the number is 7.
Careful: do not take 43 per cent of 196. 196 is only a part of the number, not the number itself.
43 per cent is 43 lots of 1 per cent. 40 times 7 is 280, and 3 times 7 is 21. Together, 301.
So 43 per cent of the number is 301.
Check: the whole number is 100 times 7, which is 700. Half of 700 is 350, and 43 per cent should be a bit less than half. 301 is. Sensible.
So to go from one per cent of a number to another, drop down to 1 per cent, then climb back up.
Medha borrowed 3500 rupees from a friend at simple interest. After 3 years she repaid the loan with 4340 rupees. What was the rate of interest per annum?

board.text: Borrowed Rs.3500. Repaid Rs.4340 after 3 years.

beats.say: 4340 rupees is called the amount. It is the 3500 rupees that was borrowed, with the interest on top.
So how do we find the interest?

ask.ifNot: The amount is the starting money and the interest together. Take the starting money away, and the interest is what is left.

beats.say: 4340 minus 3500 is 840. So the interest is 840 rupees, for all 3 years.
Careful: the rate is for one year, not for all 3. Simple interest is the same every year, so one year's interest is 840 divided by 3, which is 280.
The rate tells us what every 100 rupees earns in one year. 3500 divided by 100 is 35, so the money is 35 hundreds.

board.text: Rate = interest on each Rs.100 in 1 year

beats.say: 35 hundreds earn 280 rupees a year. Try 8: 30 times 8 is 240, and 5 times 8 is 40. Together that is 280, so each hundred earns 8 rupees.
Each 100 rupees earns 8 rupees a year. That is a rate of 8 per cent per annum.
Check with the formula: principal, times rate, times time, divided by 100. 3500 times 8 times 3, divided by 100, is 840. That is our interest.
So for the rate: amount minus principal gives the interest. Share it over the years, and then over the hundreds.
A dealer buys 26 cricket bats at 1250 rupees each. He sells 14 of them at 1800 rupees each, and the rest at 825 rupees each. Profit or loss, and what per cent?

board.text: Sold 14 at Rs.1800, the rest at Rs.825.

beats.say: First the cost. 26 bats at 1250 rupees each. 26 times 1000 is 26000, and 26 times 250 is 6500. Together, 32500 rupees.
He sold 14 bats at 1800 rupees. How many were left to sell at 825 rupees?

ask.ifNot: He had 26 bats and sold 14 of them at the higher price. The rest is 26 minus 14, which is 12 bats.

beats.say: Now his sales, as a bill. 14 bats at 1800 rupees is 25200. And the other 12 bats at 825 rupees is 9900.
Add the two lines of the bill. 25200 plus 9900 is 35100 rupees. That is the total selling price.
He paid 32500 and got 35100. More came in than went out, so it is a profit. 35100 minus 32500 is 2600 rupees.
For the profit per cent, the 2600 rupees is compared with which amount?

ask.ifNot: Profit per cent is always worked out on the cost price, all the money he paid. That is 32500 rupees.

beats.say: 1 per cent of 32500 is 325. How many 325s make 2600? 8 times 325 is 2600. So the profit is 8 per cent.
Check with a rough guess. 10 per cent of 32500 is 3250. Our profit, 2600, is a bit less than that, so 8 per cent is sensible.
So: total cost price, total selling price, the gap between them, and then the per cent on the cost price.
Mishti has marks in four subjects. Three are out of 50 and one is out of 100. We want her overall percentage.
Let us make a mark sheet. For the overall percentage we need two totals: the marks she scored, and the marks they were out of.
Add up what she scored, one line at a time. 44 plus 50 is 94. Add 42 to get 136. Add 84 to get 220.
Now the marks they were out of. 50 plus 50 plus 50 is 150, and 100 more makes 250.
She scored 220 marks. For the overall percentage, that is 220 out of what?

ask.ifNot: Three papers were out of 50 and one was out of 100. Altogether that is 250 marks, so we compare 220 with 250.

beats.say: So she has 220 out of 250. Per cent means out of 100, so shrink the 250 down to 100. Divide both by 5: 44 out of 50. Then double both: 88 out of 100.
88 out of 100 is 88 per cent.
Careful with a tempting shortcut: finding the per cent for each subject and averaging them. That does not work here, because Social Science carries more marks than the others.
Check: she lost 250 minus 220, which is 30 marks. 10 per cent of 250 is 25, so she lost a bit more than 10 per cent. 88 per cent is sensible.
So for an overall percentage: total scored, over total marks, then turn it into out of 100.
4250 rupees earns simple interest for 5 years, at 8 per cent per annum. We want the simple interest.

board.text: Rs.4250 for 5 years at 8% per annum

beats.say: 8 per cent per annum means every 100 rupees earns 8 rupees in a year. But 4250 is not a whole number of hundreds, so we go through 10 per cent.

board.text: Every Rs.100 earns Rs.8 in 1 year

beats.say: 10 per cent of 4250 is 425. And 1 per cent is 42.5, so 2 per cent is double that: 85.
We have 10 per cent and 2 per cent. How do we make 8 per cent from them?

ask.ifNot: 8 is 2 less than 10. So 8 per cent is 10 per cent, with 2 per cent taken off.

beats.say: 425 minus 85 is 340. So one year earns 340 rupees.
Simple interest earns the same each year, for 5 years. 5 times 300 is 1500, and 5 times 40 is 200. Together, 1700.
Check with the formula: principal, times rate, times time, divided by 100. It gives 1700 as well.
So the simple interest is 1700 rupees.
So: the interest for one year first, then times the number of years. And an awkward per cent can be built from easy ones.
We start with 80. Some per cent of 80 is added to it, and the sum must equal the square of 12. Which per cent?
First the target. The square of 12 is 12 times 12. 12 tens are 120, and 12 twos are 24. Together, 144.
We start at 80 and must reach 144. How do we find what has to be added?

ask.ifNot: We want the gap between where we are, 80, and where we must get to, 144. A gap is found by subtracting.

beats.say: 144 minus 80 is 64. So 64 must be added.
Careful: 64 is not the answer yet. The question asks what per cent of 80 that 64 is.
Use 10 per cent of 80, which is 8. How many 8s make 64? 8 times 8 is 64.
So 64 is 8 lots of 10 per cent. That is 80 per cent of 80.
Check: 80 per cent of 80 is 64, and 80 plus 64 is 144, the square of 12.
So: find the target, find the gap, then ask what per cent of the starting number the gap is.
An article is sold at a loss of 80 rupees. Had it been sold at 375 rupees, the profit would have been twice the loss. What was it really sold for?

board.text: Sold at a loss of Rs.80.
At Rs.375, the profit would be twice the loss.

beats.say: Everything here hangs on the cost price, the middle bar. The real sale is 80 rupees shorter than it. The sale at 375 is longer than it.
The profit would be twice the loss, and the loss is 80 rupees. So what would the profit be?

ask.ifNot: Twice means 2 times. 2 times 80 is 160.

beats.say: 2 times 80 is 160. So at 375 rupees, the profit would be 160 rupees.
A profit means 375 is above the cost price, by 160. So the cost price is 375 minus 160, which is 215 rupees.
Careful now. Is 215 our answer?

choices: No: take off the loss of 80
ask.ifNot: 215 rupees is the cost price. The article was really sold at a loss of 80, so the selling price is 80 below the cost price.

beats.say: 215 minus 80 is 135. So the article was sold for 135 rupees.
Check: from 135 up to 375 should be the loss and the profit together, 80 plus 160, which is 240. And 375 minus 135 is 240. It fits.
So find the cost price first. A profit sits above it, a loss sits below it.
28500 rupees amounts to 38760 rupees in 3 years, at simple interest. We want the rate of interest, as a per cent per annum.

board.text: Rs.28500 amounts to Rs.38760 in 3 years

beats.say: 38760 rupees is called the amount. It is the 28500 rupees that was put in, with the interest on top.
So how do we find the interest?

ask.ifNot: The amount is the starting money and the interest together. Take the starting money away, and the interest is what is left.

beats.say: 38760 minus 28500 is 10260. So the interest is 10260 rupees, for all 3 years.
Careful: the rate is for one year, not for all 3. Simple interest is the same every year, so one year's interest is 10260 divided by 3, which is 3420.
The rate tells us what every 100 rupees earns in one year. 28500 divided by 100 is 285, so the money is 285 hundreds.

board.text: Rate = interest on each Rs.100 in 1 year

beats.say: 285 hundreds earn 3420 rupees a year. 10 times 285 is 2850, and 2 times 285 is 570. Together that is 3420, so each hundred earns 12 rupees.
Each 100 rupees earns 12 rupees a year. That is a rate of 12 per cent per annum.
Check with the formula: principal, times rate, times time, divided by 100. 28500 times 12 times 3, divided by 100, is 10260. That is our interest.
So for the rate: amount minus principal gives the interest. Share it over the years, and then over the hundreds.
Here is a line with two per cents and a hidden number, M. We want M.
First we turn each per cent into a plain number. Start on the left, with 6.5 per cent of 800.
1 per cent of 800 is 8. So 6 per cent is 6 times 8, which is 48. And half a per cent is half of 8, which is 4.
6.5 per cent is 6 per cent and half a per cent together. 48 plus 4 is 52.
Now 8 per cent of 250. 1 per cent of 250 is 2.5, and 8 times 2.5 is 20.
So the line now says: 52 equals 20 plus M. Here it is on a balance.
20 plus M makes 52. How do we find M?

ask.ifNot: 20 and M together make 52. Take the 20 away from the 52, and what is left is M.

beats.say: 52 minus 20 is 32. So M is 32.
Check: 20 plus 32 is 52, and 52 is 6.5 per cent of 800. Both sides balance.
So with a line like this, turn each per cent into a plain number first. Then it is a simple missing number sum.
An article sold for 78 rupees makes a loss of 35 per cent. We want the selling price that would give a profit of 15 per cent.

board.text: Sold for Rs.78: a loss of 35%.

beats.say: The bridge between the two sales is the cost price. Call the cost price 100 per cent.
With a loss of 35 per cent, the 78 rupees is what per cent of the cost price?

ask.ifNot: A loss takes 35 per cent away from the cost price. 100 minus 35 leaves 65 per cent.

beats.say: 100 minus 35 is 65. Careful: 78 rupees is not the 35 per cent. It is the 65 per cent that is left.
Here is a neat stepping stone. 65 per cent is 13 lots of 5 per cent. And 78 divided by 13 is 6. So 5 per cent of the cost price is 6 rupees.
The cost price is 100 per cent, which is 20 lots of 5 per cent. 20 times 6 is 120 rupees.
Now the new sale. A profit of 15 per cent is 3 lots of 5 per cent. 3 times 6 is 18 rupees.
The cost price is 120 and the profit is 18. What is the new selling price?

ask.ifNot: The profit is added on top of the cost price, 120, not on top of the old selling price.

beats.say: 120 plus 18 is 138. So it should be sold for 138 rupees.
Check the first sale. 35 per cent is 7 lots of 5 per cent, 7 times 6 is 42, and 120 minus 42 is 78. It fits.
So to move from a loss sale to a profit sale, go back to the cost price first. Then build the new selling price from it.
We want to earn 280 rupees of simple interest every month. The rate is 15 per cent per annum. How much must we invest?

board.text: Interest Rs.280 every month at 15% per annum

beats.say: The interest is given per month, but the rate is per annum, per year. What must we do first?

ask.ifNot: The rate, 15 per cent, is for a whole year. So the interest must be for a whole year too: 12 months of 280 rupees.

beats.say: Careful, that is the trap in this question. A year has 12 months, so we need 12 times 280. 10 times 280 is 2800, and 2 times 280 is 560. Together, 3360.
So in one year the interest is 3360 rupees. And that is 15 per cent of the money invested.
15 per cent is 3 lots of 5 per cent. So 5 per cent is 3360 divided by 3, which is 1120.
The whole is 100 per cent, which is 20 lots of 5 per cent. 20 times 1120 is 22400. So we must invest 22400 rupees.
Check: 10 per cent of 22400 is 2240, and 5 per cent is 1120. Together that is 3360 a year. Shared over 12 months, it is 280 a month.
So match the time to the rate first: monthly interest becomes yearly interest. Then build from the known per cent up to 100 per cent.
16000 rupees is invested for 18 months, at 8 per cent per annum. We want the simple interest.

board.text: Rs.16000 for 18 months at 8% per annum

beats.say: Per annum means every year. 8 per cent means every 100 rupees earns 8 rupees in one year. And 16000 is 160 hundreds.

board.text: Every Rs.100 earns Rs.8 in 1 year

beats.say: So one year earns 160 times 8. 16 times 8 is 128, so 160 times 8 is 1280 rupees.
The rate is for a year, but the money is invested for 18 months. How long is 18 months?

ask.ifNot: A year has 12 months. 18 months is 12 months and 6 more. That is 1 year, and half a year.

beats.say: Careful, that is the trap here: the 18 is months, not years. The first year earns 1280. The extra 6 months is half a year, so it earns half of 1280, which is 640.
1280 plus 640 is 1920. So the simple interest is 1920 rupees.
Check with the formula. The time must be in years, and 18 months is 1.5 years. 16000 times 8 times 1.5, divided by 100, is 1920.
So always check the time. If it is in months, turn it into years before you use the yearly rate.
